title: When Something Fails
voice: Pablo Macias (es-MX), calmo y claro, ritmo de clase

lines.text: At Farmacy Food, when a customer confirms an order, the order moves to a state the team calls ready to pay.
That message has to reach payment processing no matter what, because selling meals is the whole business. And at the same time, they wrote, that order may end up being processed more than once.
What cannot happen is for that to end in double, triple, and further charges on a customer's account.
That it always arrives and that it is never charged twice are two demands pulling in opposite directions, and both of them are designed.

scenes.kicker: What gets designed for each message

lines.text: When the parts talk to each other through messages, some things are designed apart from the happy path, the path where everything goes well.
What happens if a message arrives twice, or is saved only halfway. How one that never arrived is retried, and what happens when the retries run out.
And what it means when a piece of data, or the whole business, goes silent.
So that a message is not lost, the queue waits for an acknowledgment. If the consumer does not report that it finished, the queue delivers the message again.
The problem is that the acknowledgment can also get lost, even though the work was done. That is why this guarantee is called at-least-once delivery, and duplicates come along with it.
Farmacy Food proposes handling the duplicate with two pieces of data that travel with the order: a unique identifier, generated by the customer's own phone, and a version number.
On processing, the system checks whether an order with that identifier already exists, and an event with a version already seen is discarded.
The cost is written down in one line. Performance drops a little, but data integrity is gained, that is, the data stays correct and nothing is lost.

scenes.kicker: Two writes that can be left half done

lines.text: There is a neighboring problem. When something happens in the business, the system has to save it in its database and also publish the event for the others.
These are two separate writes, and if the system crashes between the first and the second, the database says one thing and the rest of the system never finds out.
Farmacy Family, the health community that improves the Farmacy Food system, solved it with a well-known pattern, in two halves. The first is called outbox.
When publishing, the event is first saved in the same database, and another process sends it and marks it as sent.

The second half is called inbox, and it is the same idea on the receiving side. The event is saved first, another process handles it and marks it as handled, and that makes it possible to ignore the ones that already arrived.

MobilityCorp, on the other hand, commits the transaction when a booking is made and only then publishes the event, without saying what happens if the publish fails. That is exactly the gap this pattern covers.
ClearView sends resumes to human resources systems that go down frequently.
When a delivery fails, the request goes to a dead-letter queue and is retried with a wait that grows on every attempt, so as not to overload a system that is already in trouble.
If the failures continue, it moves to higher-level retry queues, until no more attempts are made.
And there what is written ends. In ClearView, no document says what happens to a resume after the last attempt, or who finds out that it did not arrive.
Farmacy Food does write an ending for its payment. If the app receives no confirmation that the payment was accepted or rejected, the user should be told, and should be offered a retry.
Designing for failure includes that ending: someone has to find out, and there has to be a path that does not depend on the system that failed.
Sometimes the failure is not a repeated message but one that stops arriving. In MonitorMe, if a sensor fails, the screen simply stops showing that data.
That is why the rules that analyze the patient can be configured for the case where the data does not exist or is too old: the rule does not run, or an alert fires.
And alerts go out through two different channels, to the phone and to the nursing station, so that if one is unavailable, the other gives the warning.

Farmacy Food faces the same thing with the refrigerators, which can stop sending their stock because of no network or maintenance. It proposes keeping its own estimate and correcting it when new data arrives.
And it left a question written down as pending, to be agreed with the business: when to raise an alarm over a data gap, after minutes or after hours.
There is a silence that is harder to see, the business's. Machine metrics, such as processor or memory, can say everything is fine while something in the business logic has stalled.

For that, Farmacy Food added business health checks. A supervisor sends test messages that run through the critical scenarios, for example placing an order, and measures whether the result is correct and how long it takes.
The cost is written down: those test messages have to be designed into the code, and that adds effort and complexity.
In return, the system gets one more layer of safety for the case where the machines are healthy and the business is not.
Farmacy Food's ready-to-pay order has its answers proposed in writing.
It arrives at least once, the duplicate is discarded by identifier and version, and if the payment is not confirmed, the user is told and can retry.
What began as two opposing demands, that it always arrives and that it is never charged twice, ended up resolved on paper before building anything.
Every important message in a system brings its own failure questions, and answering them in a document costs far less than discovering them with a customer who was charged twice.
